Whether this inference be true or false can in my opinion hardly be expected to make an impartial Committee decide that it outweighs long years of dangerous opposition to Nazism when the question of release from internment is considered.

The one allegation to which I have referred above is to be found at 51A in the file and derives from a source who, I am assured, is regarded as thoroughly reliable. The allegation is the bald statement that "early on in the war Walther tried to pay a visit to the Hague, which was the centre for Russian military intelligence for Western Europe up to its occupation by the Germans. At that time it was difficult to procure a visa for Holland, but he obtained a Belgian visa which was far easier and was then conveyed secretly into Holland by a Soviet mission." This statement is repeated at 50A in the course of an interview with the same informant. On neither occasion does it seem to have inspired curiosity as to how the informant came to have such knowledge and until that point is cleared up I find it very difficult to attach much importance to a statement of that kind. It sounds to me like a guess. In my opinion the informant in question ought to be interviewed again immediately and cross-examined as to the foundation for the statement.

The importance of this allegation is that it is in my opinion the only evidence of any sort of subversive activity by these brothers since their arrival in this country in 1936. The informant who makes the statement admits (50A) that another informant who has also reported on these brothers without repeating this particular allegation "has a more intimate knowledge of the LOWENHEIN's than he has".

The most recent report on the brothers (see 55B) confirms their association with the Communist Party and Russia generally but adds that the informant does not believe that the LOWENHEIN's activity was ever directed against the present or former Allied cause. It appears that there is one more informant in this country who was for a number of years the secretary of Walther LOWENHEIN in Berlin who can give valuable information about the brothers and who has not yet been found for an interview. This matter is having attention at the present moment.

The fourth informant referred to above, who is a woman at the time in internment, gave it as her opinion that Walther LOWENHEIN was a Communist but an exceedingly clever one who would always work in the background. One can only say that if this is true there is no other evidence of it in the file, and it is completely inconsistent with the man's apparent activities since 1928.

If one were compelled to give one's opinion on the case at the present stage I think one would have to admit that there is much to be said for the opinion of the Hurst Committee. It looks to me probable that up to the time of their severance of their connections with the Communist Party, which I think occurred about 1928, both brothers probably conveyed such information as they could to the Russians. I think it considerably more probable than not that they genuinely severed their connection with the Communist Party in 1938 and that their Social Democratic activities from that date until 1936 genuinely represent their political sympathies. I consider that there is no evidence worthy of the name that they have done anything to encourage suspicion since their arrival in this country. On the other hand they appear to be generally distrusted and to have a none too good business reputation, which may account for the distrust. In any case it will be pointed out by the Committee and by the Home Office that every suggestion of subversive activity against these brothers associates them with the Russians who are not our Allies and that there is nothing in their history to indicate that they would ever do anything to hinder the cause of smashing Russia. In my opinion all we can say against this argument is that if they are connected with Soviet espionage they will say for the Soviet whether the results of their espionage tells for this country or against it in the long run, but we should have to admit that so long as we remain on our present terms with the Soviet their activities are likely to be directed in our common interest.
